ONE OF THE CENTRAL AIMS of psychoanalytic treatment is to increase the patient's curiosity about himself. In short, it involves an inquiry that links surface behavior to motives that are assumed to be more deeply placed, and an understanding of the derivative distorted remnants of childhood wishes that impinge upon our thoughts, images and interaction with others. In so many ways, a psychoanalysis is an inquiry—an inquiry by two people, both involved in understanding the mind and behavior of one of the parties of the dialogue. In order for this to take place, we adopt questioning attitudes about almost everything, including the apparently most banal of behaviors such as how one walks in the door, how one sits or lies down, how one greets the other, and certainly, why we talk about this or that rather than something else.

Inquiry however, is just one specie of a large array of possible other words which relate to the notion of a questioning attitude—a question, after all, is simply a grammatical form that bears a certain syntactic arrangement that is distinctive in each language. More important to us is how that syntactic arrangement—whether it is formed by prefixing a 'wh' question which involves inversion of subject and object or simply by a rising inflection that transforms a declarative sentence into a question—affects the listener. The syntax, it seems, carries semantic importance in how it is referenced and redecoded by both the speaker and the auditor, or the analyst and the analysand. In fact, we have so many varied words in English for the word, question, and each carries very different significance and meaning. We ought to review some of them so that we can become aware of the range of distorted reception that may be evoked in a patient by merely being asked a question. ACROSS TIME AND ACROSS CULTURES, the human mind has grappled with the complexities of love. From ancient eras to the present day and in every country throughout the globe, attempts have been made to capture the essence of this innate, universal emotion. Language itself attests to this continuing centuries-old search. The sheer abundance of semantic modulations—present in ancient Greek and modern English alike—exists as evidence of our desire to define and to encompass love's varied meanings.

Ancient tongues clearly divulge the multiplicitous nature of love. The Greeks made a distinction between "eros" (sexual love, hence the English word "erotic") and "agape" agáph (the love that flourishes between friends or family members), as well as many other expressions. In the Hebrew language, numerous words were employed to describe love, in its sexual, familial, and also specifically theological connotations. The Israelite view of spiritual love spoke of the "reciprocal affection of God and people, " and indicated a unique form of love that was pure, intense, selfless, and faithful.1

The Latin word "amo" covers a range of meanings, from passionate love to brotherly love to the love between God and man and even to self-love. Rooted in the ancient Sanskrit "sam" or "kam, "2 this Latin formation finds present usage most familiarly in the French "amour" and, by logical association, in all the Romanic languages. (And the French, like the Germans, are careful to show the difference between the verbs "to love" and "to fall in love.") HOW CAN I RECALL TO YOU A man who, for 45 years, stimulated my imagination, aroused my curiosity in both personal and professional ways, who was so markedly proficient in so many areas that he was truly a Renaissance Man.

He was the first peer of mine who was divorced. He was the first person I knew who chose to live south of 59th Street. He lived a fun bohemian life at that time. He was chummy with off-beat mental health people. He kept tropical fish, he later had dogs. He found, he loved, he married Phyllis, thereby he secured for himself a beautiful, supportive companion who enjoyed him as he was and whom he enjoyed as she was. He was quietly proud, affirming the beings and the achievements of David, Josh, and Liz. He was the least ambivalent of the parents I have known. I can recall the bemused pride with which he would tell how little he understood the technical and scientific advances made by David and Josh, or the pleasure as he recounted the gaining of math skills, the mastery of foreign cultures, and the betrothal of Liz. And also the proud grandpa he was! He and his family could share off-beat vacations in Finland or on the canals of England.

WE ARE GATHERED HERE TONIGHT to share our experiences of Jack Schimel. Let me begin with one memory. In 1953 Clara Thompson invited Jack and me to join with The Financial Committee of the Board of Trustees in order to raise money for a building. Jack and I sent out a letter to the then graduates of the Institute. A couple of the answers that we received from the membership were typical analyst responses. Rather than say that they did not want to contribute money for this undertaking they asked us to document the viability of the Institute and its function in the professional world. I noted the motivation. Jack said it doesn't matter, let's just reply to them and see what happens and we did. They, of course, did not give us any money and as a matter of fact several of them left for greener pastures before we purchased the building. We purchased our present home in 1963 ten years later. If today's Society raised the equivalent amount from its present membership they would have raised $3, 000, 000. Jack helped fund this building; he entered into the pursuit of a new building for 1980 with vigor and enthusiasm. Phyllis and he gave generously to the new building fund. he said dryly in an already crackling voice, "I am a fascinating case." The last thing you want to be, he said on another occasion, is an interesting case for your doctor.

Fascinating or interesting are not words that come to me when I think of Jack. His memory is attached to moments and roles in which I have experienced his presence. My memory of him is of a friend, a man with his family and my family, in the web of all the roles in which he cut an impressive figure—teacher, healer, colleague, team-member in many years of joint purposes.

His sudden absence is numbing, the readjustment is constricting and impoverishing. Life goes on, of course. But having a Scotch, borrowing one of those awful menthol cigarettes he was so fond of, sitting quietly, feeling connected and relaxed, that simple equation is only a memory now.

My first encounter with Jack was as a candidate at the White Institute. He taught a course at his home. Those were good times, a time of learning a profession and learning the American ways in my new country. I thought that Jack's grand finale for the course with a magnificent buffet was such a wonderful example of these American ways I was eager to learn. That was the beginning of a long series of small ways I incorporated into my life which had Jack's imprimatur. When I saw that Jack had a dish of candies in his waiting room, I thought that was a swell idea. I have had one ever since. The list is long.

When life and circumstances made our lives and our families more intertwined, I came to buy the same make of car that Jack bought, the same brand of Scotch he drank, I learned to love fishing like he, I discovered the exhilaration of long walks in Scotland, England and Cape Cod. In joint family expeditions he was the captain and all our kids were happy when he approved and said good humoredly, "Good thinking." Monica, my daughter, reminds me of Jack as a benevolent but highly respected if not a little intimidatingly leader of our expeditions. His command was clear. Sometimes at 5 o'clock in the morning, he would bellow "Move out troops!" In one memorable trip along the Colorado's Great Divide we ventured onto a pass, Rollin Pass, that looked like a shortcut on the way. Deep into the pass, narrow and stony, the wall of the mountain on one side and a long drop on the other, we realized that the pass wasn't going to be a shortcut, nor could we turn around. It was rather precarious and scary.

THE IDEAL OF EGALITARIANISM WILL BE considered to mean essentially an institutionalized belief in the doctrine of equal dignity and opportunity for all. I believe that it produces pathological aspects when actual differences between persons are denied. The role of the psychoanalyst, like that of any expert in an egalitarian society, may be an uneasy one. Uneasiness may be expressed both in confessions of the limitations of the expert's field and in avowals of faith in a future statistical validation of psychoanalytic therapy.

The practice of referring a patient to several analysts, a reflection of uneasiness, seems often to be based on an egalitarian notion. One does not usually refer a patient, for example, to several cardiologists, as though the patient were as competent as the doctor to select. And yet one repeatedly sees distraught patients with lists of three or four names of analysts. Some such patients, who take literally the advice to look and choose, protest the fees or the repeated retelling involved in the selection process. It would seem that egalitarianism can be other than constructive in this context. Clara Thompson observed that certain patients who had a choice of analysts showed an uncanny ability to select the analyst least likely to disturb their neurosis. Patients can, however, exercise rational, if uninformed, judgments in this regard. My patients have chosen me for some of the following rational reasons:

1. "Your name was first on the list."

2. "Your office is the closest to the Queens-Midtown Tunnel."

3. "I preferred a Gentile." (I am not.)

4. "Your waiting room was so tiny I felt your fees would be moderate."

IN ORDER TO FACILITATE A meaningful dialogue I thought that in the time allotted to me it would be useful to highlight a few central psychoanalytic concepts which I have found particularly helpful in my work, concepts which I believe to be thoroughly embedded in a developmental point of view. So I shall be saying quite a lot about my psychoanalytic technique, but in doing so I believe that I shall also be conveying something of my own developmental perspective.

I should like to start by making some remarks about my understanding of the part played in psychic life by conflict, and to comment on the way I see its relation to development. My approach to the analytic process is very much influenced by the view that throughout life we all have to deal with continual conflicts between opposing psychic forces, and that an integral part of development is the progressive adaptations we make to these conflicts. THIS PAPER EXPLORES the process of integrating empathic mirroring within the framework of interpersonal theory. My focus will be on examining particular moments in the clinical situation in which the question arises of whether it is more effective to mirror the patient's experience or to respond in a manner that delineates the self-other aspects of the relationship. It is in the moment to moment conceptualization and clarification of such clinical choices that the practice of psychoanalysis becomes refined.

The work of Kohut has had a significant impact on psychoanalytic thinking during the past twenty years. Even analysts who strongly disagree with Kohut (as I do in many ways) often develop a position about his theories. This paper grows out of an ongoing process of my response to the clinical implications of Kohut's concept of empathic mirroring.

Perhaps the clearest example of Kohut's influence is in the area of the analyst's use of empathy. For Kohut the use of empathy was both the fundamental clinical technique for data gathering, and the organizing principle for the analytic orientation which he termed the empathic introspective mode of observation (1959). others who are depreciated, in subservience there is a facade of humility and idealization of others together with self-denigration. An apparent paucity of entitlement often masks self righteous rage and envy. I shall illustrate what I mean by subservience and its rewards with a character from Virginia Woolf's Mrs. Dalloway. I shall also describe some of my own experiences in working with a subservient patient.

By contrast with grandiosity, which I have discussed in an earlier paper (Tenzer, 1987), relatively little attention has been paid in the psychoanalytic literature to self-denigration. An exception is Horney, who describes the unconscious exaltation of inferiority, contemptibility, and submissiveness that goes along with the manifest self-minimizing, self-belittling, and self-abnegation that are the hallmark of subservience. She says that there are "taboos on all that is presumptuous, selfish and aggressive" that result in "a shrinking process." (Horney, 1950, p. 219).

A trial for the analyst is the tenacity with which this shrinking process is adhered to, the self-righteousness it entails, and the resentment it embodies. Lack of entitlement to respect and appreciation, fear of being intrusive and self-effacement are borne in exchange for a heightened sense of moral self satisfaction that is rigidly and humorlessly maintained.

The sort of person I have in mind is epitomized by Virginia Woolf's do-good governess in Mrs. Dalloway. This amanuensis, Miss Kilman, has the kind of implacable subservience that masks inordinate envy and rage. Mrs. Dalloway is described—in contrast to Miss Kilman—as having no bitterness and "none of that sense of moral virtue which is so repulsive in good women. She enjoyed practically everything" (Woolf, 1925, p. 118).

I WOULD LIKE TO PRESENT MY IDEAS in the form of a detective novel, leading you along the treatment path I traveled, describing clues as they appeared to me, allowing you to form your own hypotheses, hoping you will share my surprise as well as my confusion as the story unfolds and be intrigued by the ending. Despite some chagrin at the difficulty I had in discovering the truth about my patients situation, I believe many practitioners have been similarly misled, and that hearing my story will be useful.

The plot involves what seemed a typical case of hysterical conversion, including a charming young woman, her adored father, scorned mother and unavailable husband. A nurturing friendship turns into romance, then voila, conversion symptoms. After the analysis began however this simple paradigm broke down. The patient who seemed the paragon of health and achievement revealed layers of anxiety, fears, phobias and terror. Although she eagerly engaged in a therapeutic alliance and worked diligently inside and outside the sessions, improvement seemed more a function of feeling cared for than understood. The patterns of her behavior became clear, though the dynamics remained obscure. Her presenting symptoms vanished, only to be replaced by less tractable ones. Eventually, the untangling of the inner meaning of her symptoms and the hidden places in her personality revealed a nightmare of early childhood incest and abuse.

To begin with the latter, it strikes me that although our work puts us in a unique position to observe human lives in depth and to learn from what we have seen, as a group we are plagued by a deep uncertainty. The self-doubts are reinforced by our isolation from the academic mainstream; as a result, we are unusually vulnerable to attacks on our credibility, even when they are patently opportunistic. Recently, we have even come close to a discipline-wide intellectual panic, the "catastrophic reaction" that greeted Adolf Grünbaum's (1984) flamboyant and ultimately rather trivial attack on the validity of psychoanalytic propositions.

Because of this, we often hear that it is urgent for us to coordinate psychoanalytic observations and hypotheses with those of so-called "adjacent" disciplines. Many analysts seem to think that we can bootleg a measure of legitimacy if our findings agree with those of the neurologists, or the anthropologists, or, most recently, the developmental psychologists. In contrast, I feel a certain amount of skepticism; I suspect that we can stand on our own as a discipline, without deferring and without conceding that our findings are contingent upon those that come from other fields or that grow out of other observational methods.

Accordingly, I bristle at comments like this one from Daniel Stern contrasting the value of psychoanalytic and direct child observation:

The current scientific Zeitgeist has a certain persuasive and legitimizing force in determining what is a reasonable view of things. And at this moment the Zeitgeist favors observational methods. … As related fields, presumably about the same subject matter though from different perspectives, they will not tolerate too much dissonance, and it currently appears that it is psychoanalysis that will have to give way (1985, pp. 16–17).

Introduction

FROM THE TIME OF BIRTH, HUMAN BEINGS confront a developmental challenge unknown to other species—the attainment of an individual identity and sense of self. Since they are equipped with the capacity for consciousness—an endowment which may be viewed as both a blessing and a curse—individuals must come to terms with the realization that they are separate and distinct from others, as well as from the world around them. Recognizing one's singular status requires a process of deliberate self-definition and differentiation from the external world. Moreover, the individual must also reconcile, in some fashion, the knowledge that others may perceive of the world differently and, indeed, that certain cultural or societal norms may be contrary to one's own perspective and beliefs (Freud, 1930) ; (Fromm, 1976).

In order to negotiate a position in the physical and interpersonal realms, the individual must internalize a viable model of reality (White, 1963). This model incorporates a subjective interpretation of the interrelationships that objects and people in the world maintain with each other (Bowlby, 1988). If serious distortions occur during the construction of this model of reality, these distortions will emerge in the subsequent development of the individual's personality (Sullivan, 1953). If, however, these distortions can be isolated during the psychoanalytic process, developmental arrests may be rectified.

The task of devising a developmental model of reality may seem daunting and, indeed, it is.

THE SUBJECT OF SELFANALYSIS(the classical psychoanalytic term; see Ticho, 1967) ; (Calder, 1980) ; (Gay, 1988) ; (Chessick, 1990), which I will strictly distinguish from that of self-processing(the term I propose for the communicative version of this effort; see Langs, 1991, in press, b), has a long but sparse history. It is the main purpose of this paper to extend this literature first, by defining the method of self-processing developed through the communicative approach to psychoanalysis and psychotherapy; and second, by presenting a new professional endeavor—teaching self-processing, a new way of developing self-analytic skills and opening up fresh avenues to personal insight.

My focus will be on the classroom experience; this topic is, as far as I can discern, new to the literature. I will therefore concentrate on the definitive properties of such an encounter, and sharply distinguish the encounter itself from one of its goals—enabling the student to successfully engage in his or her own self-processing. Other aspects of this educational experience will be clarified as I proceed.

Background Literature

Self-analysis began with Freud (1897) ; (Gay, 1988) ; self-processing with the communicative approach and my own personal efforts at self-exploration (Langs & Badalamenti, in press). Freud introduced the concept of self-analysis in his letters to Fliess, stressing the high level of resistance and frustration inherent to this kind of endeavor. Nonetheless, he, and others after him (see Gay, 1988) ; (Chessick, 1990), saw the outcome of his monumental struggle as highly successful—e.g., as the means by which Freud made many of his early discoveries, including that of the Oedipus complex.

ACLINICAL EXAMPLE MAY ILLUSTRATE one facet of Erich Fromm's influence on analytic practice. Suppose that an attractive and educated thirty-eight-year-old woman consults an analyst because of concern and confusion about her own tendency to threaten her relationship with her husband and her children. Call her Emily. The husband is a personable, rising corporate executive to whom Emily has been married for fourteen years. Warm and generous to her and to their two pre-teen daughters, he consistently encourages Emily's ambivalent efforts to be recognized as a serious poet. For her part, she frankly admits that she resents what she experiences as his intense involvement in his own career. Emily realizes that she hampers his goals by refusing more than token social participation with his colleagues and their wives.

Not only the husband but the daughters, too, are upset increasingly by her curt, critical responses to his expressed desires and opinions. What precipitated Emily's decision to seek treatment was anticipation of their impending vacation alone with each other. From past holidays she knows that intensified contact heightens her sense of her husband as almost intolerably vapid. In genuine distress, she reveals her fear that her attitude may be destructive, since he has done so well in his work and is so widely valued by others.

From a Frommian perspective, the analyst might question whether the patient's self-blame is simply a matter of learned and assumed female masochism, or whether, perhaps, she also is intuitively disturbed by the value commitments of her family life.

IN A PAPER ENTITLED "The Unreasonable Patient, " Giovacchini (1985) refers to the general situation in which a patient's psychopathology clashes with the treatment process, as a psychoanalytic paradox. He puts it that "transference repetition is essential for analytic resolution but with some patients, its very nature seems to preclude analysis" (p. 8). Taking as an example, patients who seem to enact their right to be unreasonable during the course of treatment, he sees their need for enactment dominating the analytic situation, and the patient's ego as having lost its self-observing function. Clinically, this frequently results in a situation where the therapist, because he feels helpless and unable to maintain his analytic role, experiences the patient as "difficult." The paradox to which he refers is in the fact that a central part of the analytic process is for the patient to be able to experience his primitive affects and mental states in the treatment itself, and that insight formulations always contain the potential of depriving the patient of fully experiencing an affective state to its ultimate resolution.

METAPHOR NECESSARILY UNDERLIES a theory of mind. In recent years the change in the psychotherapeutic theory has been so great as to represent a paradigm shift in the Kuhnian sense. Nevertheless, the basic metaphor which underpins this emerging theoretical framework has not yet been clearly identified. What follows is an attempt to elaborate the metaphor of the "spielraum", which seems to be central to newer approaches to the understanding and treatment of personality disorder. This metaphor links to Freud's remark, written almost as an aside, in which he made an analogy between the transference and a play space ("spielraum") (Freud, 1914, p. 154). Levenson (1972), who Lifton (1976) has credited with heralding the paradigm shift, has repeatedly pointed out the significance of Freud's remark.

The metaphor of the playspace provides a new way of looking at transference phenomena, traditionally conceived as fundamental to the therapeutic process.

Ego and the Pathogenic Secret

Before proceeding to the new metaphor it is necessary to review briefly what went before it.

When Freud began to work on developing his theory of psychoanalysis, he did so in an intellectual climate which Ellenberger (1970) has outlined. One of the principal ideas forming this climate is what Ellenberger has called the "pathogenic secret". He traced the story of this model of psychological healing through a number of cultures. The patient is conceived as if he has within himself a bad experience which rots there like a malignancy. It must be removed for cure to occur.

IN THE HISTORY OF PSYCHOANALYSIS, there is a tradition of considering clinical data from multiple points of view in Freud's (1915b) metapsychological assumption's and Waelder's (1936) principle of multiple determination. After Hartmann's (1939) work on ego adaptation, Rapaport and Gill (1959) suggested that Freud's original metapsychological list should be expanded to include the economic, dynamic, topographic, structural, genetic, and adaptive points of view. Anna Freud (1965) broadened this even further into a comprehensive metapsychological profile for clinical data considering these and other viewpoints from a developmental perspective.

In this manner, Freudian theory has been able to reconsider alternative viewpoints that were first opposed and to gradually integrate them into an increasingly multi-dimensional psychoanalysis, as in the rejection of Alder's (1908) suggestion of an aggressive drive coexistent with the libido that was later incorporated into Freud's (1920) dual instinct theory. More recently, the integration of aspects of Kleinian object relations theory and Freudian ego psychology by Winnicott, Mahler, and Kernberg and Kohut's expansion of Freud's (1914) sketch on narcissism into a separate line has led to Freudian proposals to add object relations and self psychology to Freud's list of metapsychological points of view (Pine, 1990) or to Anna Freud's developmental lines (Gedo and Goldberg, 1973).

THE PURLOINED SELF REPRESENTS the heart of the work of Edgar Levenson, from the early 1970s to 1990. Most appeared originally in this journal, the home of interpersonal psychoanalysis and of Levenson. Some readers may be disappointed that there is no new writing here, but the opportunity to have the author's major work under one cover should compensate.

Levenson's papers are the right stuff to launch this new psychoanalytic publishing venture. He is the leading interpersonal psychoanalytic thinker of our era, the late 1960s to the present. This should not mask his stature in the broader span of psychoanalysis (see Hoffman, 1983).

Levenson is a brilliant writer; provocative, witty and engaging. It is difficult to remain neutral to his work for he is always challenging generally accepted notions, including those associated with interpersonal psychoanalytic lore. His contributions to interpersonal psychoanalysis rank with those of Harry Stack Sullivan, Erich Fromm, Frieda Fromm-Reichmann and Clara Thompson. Among contemporary interpersonal writers, only Benjamin Wolstein's work can compare in volume and significance.

Though one can hear echoes of each of Levenson's forebears in his voice, Clara Thompson's is the loudest. He does not share Sullivan's and Fromm-Reichmann's interest in analytic work with seriously disturbed patients, nor does he evidence Fromm's interest in integrating psychoanalysis and social thought. IMAGINE, IF YOU WILL, THE following scenes:

A patient lingers at the end of an hour. I think he is about to reach a point of closure; it seems like it will be any second. But he continues. He is in the middle of something that seems important. With what gestures and words do I interrupt him? I feel that he is very vulnerable. Should I try to explore his obliviousness to the time or his opposition to it? If I wait until the next session I may not find an opportunity to bring it up. In principle, I should be able to say something like: "I'm finding it hard to interrupt you, but we do have to stop now. You know I think the way it goes between us at the ends of sessions may have some meaning that we should explore." But within the situation itself, to say that seems very difficult.

Another patient gets up to leave two or three minutes before the end of her session. There has been no readily identifiable provocation. This is one way that she frequently deals with the separation. Should I just let her go or should I say "You know we still have a few minutes?" or "Oh sit down will you!" or, "Excuse me. Is my time up?" My focus here will be on how the nature of the analyst's participation can become the key to the question of analyzability.

The work of Winnicott (1949), (1969), Little (1951), (1957), Fromm-Reichmann (1939), (1950), (1952), and Searles (1965), among others, has been ground breaking in demonstrating that certain kinds of analyst participation can make it possible to work effectively with individuals who formerly might have been considered unanalyzable. This body of work suggests that patients are too often blamed for what may actually be the limits of their analysts or of existing theories of technique, or for what may be the analyst's unwillingness to open himself or herself to the kinds of turmoil and stress working with more difficult patients often can entail.

TO ATTEMPT TO SPECIFY "Frommian therapeutic practice" is paradoxical when Fromm rejected any prescriptive ideas. To him, the classical emphasis on technique implied a mechanical, routinized, "doing-to" approach, that aborts the uniqueness and vitality of "being with" an individual patient. Furthermore, Fromm believed no two people are alike any more than two sets of fingerprints; there are no routine cases. Thus, the analyst can achieve understanding only through allowing herself/himself to be "soaked with" (Fromm, 1960) the individual patient's feelings and being aware of her/his own capacity for similar experiences. The analyst's self-awareness and careful observation of the particular patient takes precedence over any standardized set of practices.

For Fromm, the primary goal of psychoanalysis was to enable the patient to become individuated and autonomous, with courage to transcend irrational, constricting cultural values. Since character is in large part shaped by these same values, achieving self-direction in a warped society is a difficult task that is best accomplished through an authentic encounter between analyst and patient. Fromm rejected any dogma, ritualized procedure, or a priori theory-based interpretations that deny the uniqueness and complexity of the individual patient and violate the potential for a singularly vital encounter. He was critical of existing theories, which he believed encouraged adaptation through conformity rather than self-direction, active choice and responsibility.

WE ALL HAVE OUR MYTHS of the primal ancestor. Traditional psychoanalysis has Freud: we have H. S. Sullivan. In both cases, a great deal of fancy hermeneutical footwork is necessary to maintain tradition and continuity: to show that—what the founder meant, should have meant, would have meant had he lived—is what we are claiming today. I never met Harry Stack Sullivan; he died in 1949, several years before I entered the William Alanson White Institute. However, I did work intensively and enthusiastically with many of the people who knew him well and were great proponents of his work. So, I suppose that qualifies me as an early disciple, if not a true Apostle. Someone once said—rather sourly—that one gets the disciples one deserves.1 I don't know whether Sullivan would endorse my particular brand of interpersonalism; but I do believe that what I have to say is an extrapolation of Sullivan's position.

A GREAT DEAL HAS BEEN WRITTEN ABOUT the resistances of borderline patients to ordinary analytic process. These patients present the analyst with a variety of therapeutic dilemmas because their ability to form a true working alliance is too often either fragile or non-existent.

In everyday analytic work, associations and breaks in associations are understood and then interpreted by the analyst. However, severely disturbed patients are not always able to participate in the analysis of the associative process. Instead, they sometimes spend seemingly endless sessions attacking themselves, the analyst, or analysis itself. They may recount bitter complaints about the quality of their lives with apparently no interest in understanding anything new about the cause of their unhappiness. The analyst's attempts to offer help are met with dissatisfaction or rage. Even when these patients appear to receive help with pleasure, they often return to the next session feeling much worse, unable to connect this reaction to the analyst's intervention or to anything else. Borderline patients may react to even tentative interpretations with intense, uncontrolled aggressive outbursts, suicidal gestures or actions, or by abruptly terminating treatment. They often reject attempts by the analyst to remain neutral or to express empathy. The analyst may thus be left feeling as if all analytic tools have been exhausted (cf. Robbins, 1988) ; (Gabbard, 1989).

The patient who maintains an intensely and unremittingly hostile stance toward the analyst inevitably evokes strong countertransference feelings.

I WANT TO CONSIDER A SYNDROME WHICH becomes apparent with some clarity in the psychoanalytic psychotherapy of certain adolescent boys. While the cause of the problem is quite specific and involves the patient and his family, in particular his father, the behavior which characterizes the patient and his family is general and nonspecific. As a result, the phenomenon may go unnoticed and untreated for a long while. After a period of some work, a particular dynamic emerges which distinguishes these adolescents' depressions from other types of adolescent depressions. Further, the organization of symptoms, dynamics, and behavior have implications for the study of the father-son dyad in child development.

The father-son dyad is a relatively unstudied relationship in psychoanalysis (cf. Cath & Gunsberg, 1989), although much has been studied about the role of the father, as person, presence, and symbol, in the triadic Oedipal relationship (Blos, 1985).

IN AN ANALYTIC CONTROL SEMINAR a psychotherapist with nearly 20 years of clinical experience is presenting a case. The patient previously had been in twice weekly psychotherapy with the same therapist but the presentation is about her first analytic hour on the couch. As the protocol is reported, one has the clear impression that the patient is getting increasingly anxious about her sense of abandonment in this new circumstance. While other themes can be discerned, the assessment of both the analyst and the members of the seminar is that the patient is becoming panicky about the apparent differences between this new way of working and the old. As her anxiety mounts, the analyst makes a comment that conveys to the patient a sense that, despite the changed circumstances, she is still with her in the room. The analyst's comment has a palpable effect and the patient settles down and discusses, in what appears to be a genuine and reflective way, her decision to undertake analysis at this point and what she hopes from it.

IN THIS PAPER I DESCRIBE an interpersonal technique I have adapted for psychoanalytic work with eating disordered patients: particularly members of that subgroup who, for reasons having to do with their "false self" character defenses, are highly resistant to any direct discussion of the transference or the therapeutic relationship. At the same time I relate this specific technical application to a more general topic in the recent psychoanalytic literature: the question of how technically to approach patients whose "resistance to awareness of the transference" (Gill, 1979) ; (1982) makes them unable to tolerate standard psychoanalytic techniques such as analysis of transference and resistance.

Merton Gill coined the phrase "resistance to awareness of the transference" to refer to the pervasive tendency of psychoanalytic patients to unconsciously defend against their immediate affective responses to the therapist via such mechanisms as displacement and identification (Gill, 1980, p. 273). To deal with this kind of resistance Gill recommends that the therapist/analyst be as aggressive as possible in pursuing the transference implications of the patient's communications, even when there is no explicit reference to the therapist or therapeutic relationship. The aim of this approach is to "encourage the transference to expand within the analytic situation" (1982, pp. 59–68)

I am indebted to James W. Anderson, Mary E. Connors, Merton M. Gill, James P. Gustafson, Craig Johnson, Laura B. Kavesh, Kenneth M. Newman and Peter Barglow for their thoughtful comments on earlier versions of this manuscript.

MY FIRST CONTACT WITH JACK came 23 years ago, when he called to ask if I would accept the editorship of our journal. I believe, with the urging of Nat Stockhamer, he had read my CV, which contained the irrelevant trivia that after the Second World War I had worked for a short time on a small-town newspaper, and had had some experience with industrial magazines, before I had gone back to school. I think it was Jack's focus on the practical, and his utter confidence in the real, that pushed him to propose my name to the Executive Committee of the Institute. It might have been delusive, but I suppose he thought I had some potential. Later, when it turned out that he too was a graduate of city-desk journalism, we showed our affinity and affection for each other whenever we found ourselves together.

Although it may be difficult to believe, I tended to be somewhat diffident in those days, and, soon after his call, at a meeting of some committee, I wondered aloud how I could include all the names of a newly proposed Publication Committee on the masthead of the Journal. Jack said, with characteristic, puzzle-solving directness, and aplomb, "Use smaller type!" From then on I was on my own, and I knew that Jack and I seemed to think similarly. Jack had one abiding question which was: Was it (anything) good for the Institute?

About this time, Jack asked me for some advice about the Newsletter, of which he had assumed editorship. On this project too, we became fast friends and colleagues. The Newsletter's staff met at least four times a year at Jack's home (it was a quarterly in those days), and, separately, so did Jack and I, to put the thing together.

Nostalgia is a product of dissatisfaction and rage. It's a settling of grievances between the present and the past. The more powerful the nostalgia the closer you come to violence. War is the form nostalgia takes when men are hard-pressed to say something good about their country.
D. DeLillo, White Noise

AREADER'S INITIAL REACTION MAY be to reject this quotation as pop psychology, a misreading of a state of mind dominated by a painful, brooding, often bittersweet mood, a yearning for Eden. On the contrary, there is here an intuitively derived veracity. We may ask why these components of nostalgia are so readily overlooked.

The word derives from the Greek ("return home" and "pain") and this enduring, complex feeling tone is one that pervades many lives and motivates behavior. A notable literary exemplar is Proust's writings (1981), where the rage and grievances are carefully masked behind social satire, mockery, and the effects on the reader of the frustrations of the central characters. Clinical instances are often obscured in the workings of transference. Transference is often driven by nostalgia, not omitting the pressures of conflictual and developmental anxieties. It contains the distorted, symbolized and metaphorized strivings of the individual to live through a past that has been unsatisfying and anxiety-provoking and to nullify a subjective present that does not measure up to the real or imagined past. The patient is drawn repeatedly to bring closure to the unfulfilled; the settling of grievances is a part of these processes. It is illusionary to regard nostalgia solely as unconflicted desire for Paradise.

A distraught young woman tells me in her analytic session of the loss of her pocketbook, and it is at first unclear whether the purse was robbed from her or was inadvertently left behind at some unremembered place.

The Suicide

AS IS WELL KNOWN, VINCENT VAN GOGH ended his life with suicide. The last year-and-a-half of his life were spent in a struggle with a probable schizophreniform psychosis that began with his cutting off of his left ear lobe and required his hospitalization. During the period of Vincent's illness, suicide was never far from his mind. If we regard his lifelong pattern of self-deprivation and self-mortifications as suicidal equivalents (Menninger, 1938), the idea must have had its place through most of his life. Certainly the amputation of his ear was a suicidal gesture, or the equivalent.

During his hospitalization, there were other attempts: Paul Signac recalled an attempt during his visit in March 1889 when Vincent tried to drink some turpentine: "The whole day he spoke to me about painting, literature, socialism. That night he was a little tired. There was a frightful mistral blowing which might have unnerved him. He wanted to drink a liter of oil of turpentine out of a bottle that sat on the table in the room. It was time to return to the hospital" (Stein, 1986, p. 136). In the sanitarium there were several other occasions when he tried to swallow kerosene or oil paints and had to be forcibly restrained. It was not as though death came upon Vincent by stealth; he actively pursued it, sought it out.

Vincent was well aware that his condition was gradually worsening. There came a quiet Sunday morning. He walked out on the countryside and turned onto a small farm. He went behind the barn, and concealing himself behind a manure pile he pulled out a revolver and shot himself in the chest.

THE NOTION OF THE COUNTERTRANSFERENCE has undergone considerable transformation and elaboration since Freud first introduced it in his 1910 lectures to the Second Psychoanalytic Congress (1914). At that time, Freud restricted the concept to the influence that the patient's transferences may have on the analyst's unconscious feelings. Cautioning particularly that the analyst's reactions to the patient's erotic feelings might impair the analyst's objectivity, Freud's view of countertransference emphasized its possible dangers.

Yet countertransference as it was originally narrowly defined is only one type of emotional reaction that an analyst can have to a patient. In the 1940's, Freud's narrow definition was challenged by a number of writers, (Winnicott, 1949) ; (Heimann, 1950) ; (Racker, 1949) ; (Little, 1951) ; (and Tower, 1956). These authors and others suggested that such reactions as the analyst's own transferences, identifications and realistic reactions might all be included under the rubric of countertransference. Thus, Laplanche and Pontalis (1973) have suggested that an analyst might have transference reactions to his patients such that he responds to them as if to significant persons from his early life. Alternatively, an analyst might respond to a patient by identifying with the patient or might experience the patient as an idealized object; or as an extention of himself. Such writers as Bion (1963) held that responses are deposited in the analyst's psyche by the patient through projective identification, and thus that the analyst becomes the container of the patient's wishes. THERE IS A DIFFERENCE BETWEEN recognition that the ultimate justification of our commitment to scientific method and scientific knowledge, as well as to moral and aesthetic values does not rest on anything but that commitment itself, and the inference that one commitment is as good as another. Commitments to courses of action, beliefs and evaluations, have consequences which require renewal of commitments or their alteration. Consequences matter. Richard Rorty would agree. But then, if consequences matter, why does Rorty deny scientific method and scientific knowledge a preferred epistemological position in relation to, say, literature? Literature is a valued product of the human imagination, useful for its intended purposes, but hardly as reliable a guide to intelligent action as the scientific pursuit of knowledge. One is led to think of Peirce's insistence that no intuition—literary or otherwise—is self-justifying.

It will be argued in this paper not only that Rorty is an historicist—a classification he accepts, but also that his position is one of relativism—something he prefers to deny. Further, I intend to rebut what I regard as the deleterious consequences of Rorty's relativism for ethics—the implication that there can be no cross-cultural criteria of moral values. As a psychotherapist, I do not look to those findings for help in doing psychotherapy, or for answers to questions that come to my mind as I do psychotherapy. IN THIS PAPER I PROPOSE TO DEAL with the manoeuver by which people try to mitigate their envy by converting differences into similarities, leaving for themselves the far more possible task of merely getting or doing or being more of the same. These are people for whom the expression Vive la différence! most decidedly does not apply. For it to apply the differences they encounter must be and have been complementary, reciprocal: the one's hungry mouth—the other's providing breast; the one's excited genital—the other's also excited genital. Such mutuality of reciprocation enables the one to take and give pleasure from, and so in what he or she possesses. Where that complementation does not take place, the longing inverts toward a turn-about. Failing to find pleasure and satisfaction in what one has, one's longings to have what the other has increases proportionately. What is one's own is being wasted, and what the other has is wasted on them. First greed to have both and then envy of the other for having what one has longed to receive from and now longs to own and control comes to the fore. To have a mouth and an appetite for being fed and suckled when there is too little pleasure from leaves one with no great pleasure in. To have the breast thus seems preferable.

He knew the difference between therapy and analysis. Diagnosis prescribed the form of treatment. As therapist, he used himself decisively and authoritatively. To a depressed, deprived lad, bullied by peers, he taught magic tricks. These for the lad became a hobby, eased loneliness, provided self-esteem and eventually led to the respect of others. When Jack believed individual therapy would benefit an adolescent, he cleared the field for therapy, telling parents that their teen would do the work in therapy, if they remained themselves (i.e., not to change and present new relational challenges), paid the bills, and called him in crisis.

His paradigm of psychoanalysis was Férenczi's, as delineated by Izette de Forrest.1 This included establishing and maintaining an emotional relationship between analyst and patient, keeping up dramatic dialogue and dramatic tension, offering the analyst and analysis as battleground and playground for the patient to use for self-expression and discovery, and for testing the limits of the analyst, to reach towards his or her own potentials.

First the therapist must enable the patient to prehend—not just comprehend, rather apprehend—care. Focussing on the immediate moment leading to the call for the first appointment, the life circumstances and personal relationships surrounding this decision, and expectations of help would facilitate this. I WANT TO TALK ABOUT SELF-CONSCIOUSNESS as one form of shame, a form that emerges specifically in the encounter with the other. One of the major goals of most forms of therapy is to make the patient, in one way or another, more aware of himself. Our therapeutic expectation is, that becoming conscious of something is a way towards mastery and integration. However, this is not always the case, particularly when we consider self-consciousness. Self-consciousness is a way of becoming conscious that can lead to inhibition, paralysis and even the loss of the capacity for thinking. This is a problem that may bring people into therapy, but unfortunately it is also a problem that gets very much in the way of therapy. When a patient becomes extremely inhibited or avoidant in therapy, I sometimes think of it as a kind of stage fright, in which the patient functions as though he is afraid to perform. In this metaphorical sense, the dramatic term 'stage fright' may illustrate the force with which self-consciousness can paralyze the treatment setting. An illustration from fiction may illustrate the point.

In his 1810 essay, "On the Marionette Theater, " the German Romantic writer Heinrich von Kleist (1959) relates an episode in the life of a young man in which self-consciousness is dramatized in the context of a social interaction. After going for a swim with an older friend, the young man tells his friend about an observation he had made of himself. As he was drying himself by the side of the lake he had noticed in the reflection of the water his mirror image as it seemed to resemble the well known classical sculpture of an athlete pulling a splinter from his foot. The older friend who tells this story continues:

… Indeed at this very moment I had seen the same, but either to test the certainty of the grace residing in him or to tone down somewhat his vanity, I laughed and replied that he must be seeing ghosts. He blushed and lifted his foot a second time to show me. But the attempt as one might have foreseen misfired. Confused he lifted his foot a third and fourth time, maybe all together ten times. In vain! He was unable to reproduce the same movement. What can I say?

Clinical phenomena may be defined as "phenomena that go on between the observer and the observed in the situation created by the observer participating with the observed …" (Sullivan, 1940, p. 12). In particular, such phenomena include the patient's "verbal report of subjective appearances" (Sullivan, 1938, p. 34).

SINCE ITS INCEPTION MORE THAN A CENTURY ago, psychoanalysis has spawned diverse theoretical models and methods. Nevertheless, two aspects of this treatment remain universal—the use of the patient's narrative to communicate material to the analyst and the resurrection of memories from the patient's early life experience.

Spence (1989) has described the compelling nature of the patient's narrative by commenting that "part of our sense of self depends on our being able to go backwards and forwards in time and to weave a story about who we are, how we got that way, and where we are going: a story that is continuously nourishing and self-satisfying" (pp. 521–522). Most patients attribute great significance to their narrative disclosures, casting themselves as omniscient story-tellers in the portrayal of their past experiences and future aspirations.

In addition to this story-telling quality, psychoanalysis has also emphasized the value of retrospective information, the ability "to go backwards … in time and to weave a story about who we are and how we got that way." Indeed, in explaining the transforming effect of psychoanalysis, Freud emphasized that the patient would need to resurrect the past in order to confront and resolve long suppressed infantile desires (Freud, 1900), (1937a).

1. The Humanism of Erich Fromm

EACH PSYCHOTHERAPY EXPRESSES A CONCEPT of man and puts it into practice using methods that draw upon a background of knowledge and convictions, which in turn, is increased by the experience of clinical work. Fromm's psychotherapeutic approach matured during his lengthy career as a psychoanalyst, constantly growing, providing the indispensable support to his theoretical convictions. He declares (1962, G.A. IX, p. 43) that in his written work he never lost sight of the critical observation of human behavior which he made during his psychoanalytic work. Fromm, however, also draws upon his experience in another laboratory, the historical scene. He was born in 1900 in Frankfurt and died in 1980 in Muralto, Switzerland. He witnessed dramatic events in his Jewish childhood. A scholar of social phenomena, he is recognized as being particularly expert in two historical periods (Heller, 1978): the growth of Nazism, and the American consumer democracy. These periods provide his multidisciplinary inquiry with signal traits of the human condition leading to more general considerations which transcend the subject matter from which they derive.

Fromm's complex background—psychoanalysis, anthropology, sociology, economics, religion—does not fully explain his originality as an intellectual, which is characterized by his expression in modern day language, of teachings, which have been voiced by the Masters—biblical prophets, Socrates, Buddah, Christ, Mystic Christians, Spinoza, Marx, Albert Schweitzer, Gandhi—in the spirit of acceptance, faith, and hope which characterizes every humanistic vision (Biancoli, 1983).
